blocks.text: 1. Quantization

blocks.alt: FP32 weights are quantized into INT8 weights

blocks.text: A trained deep network's own weights, already covered generally across this course, are the raw numbers that define its behavior. Quantization, the process of representing those weights with fewer bits than they were trained with, changes how those numbers get stored and used.
It genuinely trades a small amount of numerical precision for genuinely real gains in speed and memory, a tradeoff explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Recapping Floating Point Precision
Deep networks are genuinely trained using floating point numbers. This connects back to gradient descent needing fine-grained updates, already covered generally in Training Deep Networks.
Typically 32-bit floating point is used, offering genuinely high numerical precision, the genuinely default starting point that quantization, already covered in this topic, later reduces.
3. Why Full Precision Is Expensive

blocks.alt: FP32 weights require high memory and compute

blocks.text: This connects back to floating point precision, already covered in this topic. Every single weight genuinely consumes 4 whole bytes of memory at full 32-bit precision.
A genuinely large model with billions of weights genuinely demands enormous memory and compute just to store and use them, a genuinely real, practical cost explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 4. Reducing Bit Width
This connects back to why full precision is expensive, already covered in this topic. Quantization genuinely reduces each weight down to 8-bit, or even 4-bit, integers instead of full 32-bit floats.

This genuinely cuts memory footprint dramatically while keeping the network's overall structure the exact same, a genuinely powerful, structure-preserving reduction explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Mapping Floats To Integers

blocks.alt: A float value is scaled and mapped into an integer value

blocks.text: This connects back to reducing bit width, already covered in this topic. A genuinely simple scale and offset formula maps the original floating point range onto integers.
This is genuinely reversible enough that computations can still approximate the original floating point behavior, the genuinely core mathematical trick explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This mapping formula, already covered in this topic, directly explains why quantized models can still run the exact same network architecture, already covered generally across this course, with only integer arithmetic.

blocks.text: 6. Quantization Error

blocks.alt: An original value and a quantized value have a small difference

blocks.text: This connects back to mapping floats to integers, already covered in this topic. This mapping genuinely cannot represent every single original value exactly.

The genuinely small resulting difference is called quantization error, a real cost explored throughout the rest of this topic and directly weighed against the memory and speed gains already covered earlier here.
7. Post-Training Quantization Versus Quantization-Aware Training

blocks.alt: Post-training quantization is compared against quantization-aware training

blocks.text: This connects back to quantization error, already covered in this topic. Post-training quantization genuinely applies this reduction after training already finished, directly on the already-trained weights.

Quantization-aware training genuinely simulates that same reduced precision during training itself instead, letting the network genuinely adapt to it and often reducing the quantization error already covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This distinction, already covered in this topic, directly explains why quantization-aware training often achieves genuinely lower quantization error, already covered earlier in this topic, than post-training quantization alone.

blocks.text: 8. Deployment Tradeoffs
This connects back to reducing bit width, already covered in this topic. Genuinely smaller, faster models can run on genuinely more constrained hardware, such as mobile devices or edge sensors.
This comes at the genuine cost of the small accuracy drop already covered as quantization error in this topic, a genuinely real tradeoff weighed on every real deployment decision.
9. Recognizing When Quantization Is Genuinely Worth Applying

blocks.alt: Needing a smaller, faster model points toward quantization

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely needing to deploy on constrained, edge hardware, already covered in this topic. Quantization, already covered in this topic, directly enables exactly that deployment.

This connects back to genuinely needing the absolute highest possible accuracy instead, already covered in this topic. Full precision, already covered, remains the genuinely safer choice when accuracy matters most.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates mapping floating point weights to 8-bit integers, already covered in this topic, and measuring the resulting quantization error.

code.content:
def quantize(weights, bits=8):
    # already covered as mapping floats to integers in this topic
    qmin, qmax = 0, 2 ** bits - 1
    wmin, wmax = min(weights), max(weights)
    scale = (wmax - wmin) / (qmax - qmin)

    quantized = [round((w - wmin) / scale) for w in weights]
    dequantized = [q * scale + wmin for q in quantized]
    return quantized, dequantized

weights = [0.12, -0.87, 0.45, 0.03, -0.29, 0.91]  # already covered as 32-bit floating point weights in this topic

quantized, dequantized = quantize(weights, bits=8)
print(f"Original weights (already covered as full precision in this topic): {weights}")
print(f"Quantized 8-bit integers (already covered as reducing bit width in this topic): {quantized}")
print(f"Dequantized approximation: {[round(d, 3) for d in dequantized]}")

# already covered as quantization error in this topic
error = [round(abs(o - d), 4) for o, d in zip(weights, dequantized)]
print(f"\nQuantization error per weight (already covered in this topic): {error}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows each dequantized weight landing close to, but not exactly at, its original floating point value, exactly the small quantization error already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Quantization represents a trained network's weights with fewer bits than they were trained with.
Deep networks are typically trained using 32-bit floating point, a high-precision default.
Full precision weights consume real memory and compute, which grows with every added weight.
Quantization reduces weights down to 8-bit or 4-bit integers while keeping the network structure the same.
A scale and offset formula maps the original floating point range onto integers, and back again.
This mapping is imperfect, producing a small quantization error between original and dequantized values.
Post-training quantization applies reduction after training; quantization-aware training simulates it during training.
Quantized models run faster on more constrained hardware, at the cost of a small accuracy drop.
Quantization suits constrained deployment; full precision suits tasks where accuracy matters most.
